title: VATS bullectomy with pleurodesis
subtitle: Definitive surgery for recurrent or persistent pneumothorax

sources.title: British Thoracic Society Guideline for pleural disease
ERS task force statement: diagnosis and treatment of primary spontaneous pneumothorax

indications: Recurrent spontaneous pneumothorax, ipsilateral or contralateral.
Persistent air leak or failure of the lung to re-expand despite adequate chest drainage, after discussion with the thoracic surgical team.
A first pneumothorax in a patient whose occupation or activities make recurrence dangerous (for example pilots and divers), or bilateral or tension presentation, by individual decision.
contraindications: Inability to tolerate one-lung ventilation or general anaesthesia, where medical pleurodesis or an ambulatory device may be preferred.
Dense obliterating pleural adhesions from previous surgery or infection, which may require an open approach.
Secondary pneumothorax in severe lung disease, where the decision is individual and the risk higher; this procedure outline is for primary disease.
preparation: Chest radiograph and CT where available to identify bullae, the extent of disease and the contralateral lung.
Smoking cessation advice: smoking increases recurrence.
An intercostal drain in place before induction if a pneumothorax is present, to prevent tension with positive-pressure ventilation.
Agree with the anaesthetist on a double-lumen tube or bronchial blocker, and regional analgesia (paravertebral or serratus plane block, or epidural).

Consent risks to discuss: recurrence (lower after surgical pleurodesis than after medical treatment but not zero); prolonged air leak; bleeding and the need to convert to an open thoracotomy; chronic chest wall pain and numbness; wound infection; for pleurectomy, the difficulty of future thoracic surgery on that side.
positioning: Lateral decubitus with the operated side up, an axillary roll below the dependent axilla, and the table broken to open the intercostal spaces.
Arms supported with the upper arm forward and up, pressure points padded, and the patient secured before any tilt.
equipment: Thoracoscope (usually 30 degree), camera and light, with thoracotomy instruments open and available.
Endoscopic staplers with appropriate loads, and buttress material if used.
Pleural abrasion pad or scourer, and instruments for parietal pleurectomy.
Chest drains and an underwater seal or digital drainage system.
anatomy: Blebs and bullae in primary spontaneous pneumothorax are most often at the lung apex, and sometimes at the apex of the lower lobe.
The intercostal neurovascular bundle runs in the groove on the lower border of each rib, so instruments pass over the upper border of the rib below.
At the apex, the subclavian artery and vein, the sympathetic chain with the stellate ganglion, and the brachial plexus lie just beyond the parietal pleura.
The phrenic nerve runs on the pericardium anterior to the hilum; the diaphragm rises high in expiration, so low ports can enter the abdomen.
criticalSafety: Do not induce positive-pressure ventilation with an undrained pneumothorax.
Confirm lung isolation before the first port; poor isolation makes the operation unsafe.
Insert the first port under vision or by blunt finger dissection, not by a blind trocar thrust.
Staple across normal lung beyond the bulla, never through it.
Keep pleurectomy and abrasion clear of the apex vessels, the sympathetic chain and the phrenic nerve.
Convert early for bleeding that cannot be controlled thoracoscopically.
structuresAtRisk: Sympathetic chain and stellate ganglion (Horner syndrome)
Long thoracic nerve at port sites
Diaphragm, liver and spleen with a low port
commonErrors: Missing a second bleb because the whole lung was not inspected.
Stapling too close to the bulla, so the staple line tears.
Abrading or stripping right up to the apex and injuring the stellate ganglion or subclavian vessels.
Drains placed without an apical drain, leaving an apical space.
Not repeating the leak test after the final staple line.
complications: Haemothorax from intercostal vessels, the pleurectomy bed or adhesions.
Chronic post-surgical chest wall pain and numbness.
Wound and pleural infection; re-expansion pulmonary oedema.
postop: Daily drain review: air leak, drainage volume and radiograph. Suction per surgeon and unit practice.
Remove the drain when the air leak has stopped and the lung is fully expanded.
Multimodal analgesia with regional techniques and early mobilisation and chest physiotherapy.
Advise on smoking cessation, on air travel after full resolution per BTS advice, and on lifelong avoidance of diving unless cleared by a specialist.

steps.emphasis: Confirm and mark the side against the radiographs. Include conversion to thoracotomy, recurrence and chronic pain.
State that a drain is in place if a pneumothorax is present, and the lung isolation plan.
Lateral decubitus, axillary roll, table broken; recheck tube position after turning.
Prepare widely enough for a thoracotomy and for drain sites, from the spine to the sternum.
Inspect the staple line, port sites, adhesion beds and any pleurectomy bed under the camera as the lung re-expands.
An apical drain through a port site, positioned under vision; a second basal drain if there was bleeding or the space is large.
Send the resected lung for histology; occasionally it shows an unexpected diagnosis.
Close muscle and skin at port sites in layers around the drain.
Record bullae found and resected, the pleurodesis method and its extent, the leak test, drains and suction plan.

step.vats.lung-isolation.title: Lung isolation and one-lung ventilation
step.vats.lung-isolation.why: Thoracoscopy needs a collapsed lung to see and to work. A misplaced tube gives a lung that will not deflate, a poor view, hypoxia, and pressure to work blind.
how: Ensure an intercostal drain is in place if a pneumothorax is present before positive-pressure ventilation begins.
Agree with the anaesthetist on a double-lumen tube or bronchial blocker; position is confirmed by fibreoptic bronchoscopy.
Recheck tube position after turning the patient lateral, and confirm isolation and saturation before making the first incision.
pitfalls: Starting the operation with partial lung collapse and hoping it improves.
Not rechecking the tube after positioning, when it often moves.

step.vats.ports.title: Port placement
step.vats.ports.why: The first port enters a chest that may contain adherent lung, and a low port can enter the abdomen. Ports placed to triangulate on the apex make the bullectomy and pleurodesis straightforward.
how: Place the camera port in a lower intercostal space in the mid-axillary line, entering by blunt dissection over the upper border of the rib and confirming with a finger that the lung is free.
Under vision, place working ports to triangulate on the apex, or use a single utility incision for a uniportal approach.
Divide any adhesions near the ports first, with attention to bleeding from chest wall adhesions.
structuresAtRisk: Lung adherent to the chest wall
pitfalls: A sharp trocar pushed blindly through the chest wall.
Ports placed too close together, which clash at the apex.

step.vats.inspection.title: Systematic inspection and finding the leak
step.vats.inspection.why: Recurrence after surgery often comes from a bleb that was never found. The whole lung surface, not only the obvious apical bulla, must be inspected.
how: Inspect the apex of the upper lobe, the apex of the lower lobe, the fissures and the mediastinal and diaphragmatic surfaces in a fixed order.
Divide adhesions under vision, sealing vascular ones, to free the apex.
If no bleb is seen, fill the chest with warm saline and ask for gentle ventilation of the lung to look for bubbles.
pitfalls: Stopping at the first bulla found.
Tearing lung when dividing adhesions bluntly.

step.vats.bullectomy.title: Stapled bullectomy
step.vats.bullectomy.why: Removing the diseased apical lung removes the source of the leak. A staple line through diseased tissue leaks and fails; a staple line across normal lung holds.
how: Grasp the bulla gently, or the lung just beyond it, and position the stapler across normal lung proximal to the bulla.
Choose a staple load suitable for the lung thickness; use buttress material if the lung is thin and the unit uses it.
Fire successive loads with overlapping lines and inspect the staple line for gaps and bleeding.
structuresAtRisk: Segmental vessels close to the hilum with a deep staple line
pitfalls: Taking too much lung, especially in a patient with secondary lung disease.

step.vats.pleurodesis.title: Pleurodesis: pleural abrasion or apical pleurectomy
step.vats.pleurodesis.why: Bullectomy alone leaves a significant recurrence rate. Creating adhesion between lung and chest wall is what makes the result durable.
how: For mechanical abrasion, rub the parietal pleura with an abrasion pad until it bleeds lightly, over the upper chest wall and apex.
For apical pleurectomy, raise a flap of parietal pleura along a line through the intercostal spaces and strip it from the upper chest wall, staying clear of the apex vessels.
Keep away from the sympathetic chain along the vertebral bodies, the subclavian vessels at the apex and the phrenic nerve on the mediastinum.
Chemical pleurodesis with talc is used by some units as an adjunct; follow local policy, especially in young patients.
pitfalls: Stripping or abrading over the apex dome and the sympathetic chain.
Bleeding from the pleurectomy bed that is not controlled before closure.

step.vats.leak-test.title: Leak test and re-expansion under vision
step.vats.leak-test.why: An air leak found now can be stapled or sutured in a minute; found after closure it becomes days of drainage or a return to theatre.
how: Fill the chest with warm saline over the staple lines and ask the anaesthetist to ventilate the lung gently at a sustained pressure.
Look for bubbles from the staple line and the lung surface, and repair significant leaks with staples or sutures.
Watch the lung re-expand fully under the camera before final closure.
pitfalls: Over-inflating fragile lung during the test and causing a new leak.
Accepting incomplete re-expansion because of a trapped segment that was not freed.

step.vats.conversion.title: Conversion to thoracotomy
step.vats.conversion.why: Conversion is not failure. Bleeding from a major vessel, dense adhesions or a lung that cannot be isolated are safer open, and the decision is best made early, before blood obscures the view.
how: Convert for uncontrolled bleeding, dense adhesions that cannot be divided safely, failure of lung isolation, or a finding that needs a larger resection.

For major bleeding, apply direct pressure with a sponge stick through a port, tell the anaesthetist, call for senior help and blood, and open through a lateral or anterior thoracotomy incorporating a port.
Record the reason for conversion in the operative note.
pitfalls: Persisting thoracoscopically with a poor view and rising blood loss.
Removing the pressure to look before the team, the blood and the instruments are ready.
